title: Develop, check, maintain, confirm in an agile project
blurb: Describe the four steps of the business case technique and how an agile project applies them iteratively, with benefits confirmed early and often.
question: In an agile project, some benefits start to appear after the second release, long before closure. Which step of the business case technique covers assessing them, and when does it mostly happen?

teach.body: PRINCE2 manages the business case with a four-step technique: develop, check, maintain and confirm. PRINCE2 Agile keeps the technique and applies it to the project canvas. Because an agile project releases products in increments, the steps repeat: the canvas is checked and maintained as releases land, and some benefits can be confirmed during the project rather than waiting until the end.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 6.3.1, Figure 6.3; PRINCE2 7 manual 5.3.1

teach.caption: In agile the loop turns with each stage and release, not once.

steps.label: Project manager
steps.sub: with the team, a more detailed canvas (initiating)

steps.label: Project board
steps.sub: checks it when authorizing initiation, project, stages

steps.label: Project manager
steps.sub: updates it at each stage boundary

steps.label: Project board
steps.sub: confirms the updated canvas at closure

teach.body: The principle 'ensure continued business justification' needs a valid justification throughout the life cycle. Releasing increments gives real evidence of value early, so the board can check that the project is still worthwhile using actual results, not only forecasts. If it no longer is, the board can instruct premature closure instead of authorizing the next stage.

Millbrook Hospital Trust is building an outpatient check-in app. In starting up, executive Helen Marsh leads the project canvas from the mandate (develop). The board checks it when authorizing initiation and again when authorizing the project. After release 2, check-in queues are already shorter, so project manager Daniel Mensah records the measured benefit (confirm) and, at the stage boundary, updates the canvas with actual costs and new forecasts (maintain). At closure the board confirms the updated canvas.

teach.text: 'Confirm' is not only an end-of-project step in agile. Confirming benefits mostly happens after closure, but benefits may be realized and assessed during the project when products are released iteratively. Also, 'check' asks whether the project is still worthwhile; updating the canvas with actuals and forecasts is 'maintain'.

items: Four steps: develop, check, maintain, confirm, applied to the project canvas.
Develop: explore options and get information for investment decisions.
Check: is the project (still) worthwhile? Done at each board authorization.
Maintain: update with actual progress and forecasts, e.g. at stage boundaries.
Confirm: have intended benefits been (or will they be) realized?
Agile: confirm mostly after closure, but early releases let some benefits be confirmed during the project.

summary: You can now name the four steps of the business case technique and say what each does. You can also explain how an agile project repeats them, with benefits confirmed early and often.

A.q: Which step of the business case technique means exploring options and getting the right information for investment decisions?
A.why: Develop means exploring options and getting the right information upon which investment appraisal decisions can be made (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Check assesses whether the project is still worthwhile.
whyNot.1: Confirm assesses whether intended benefits have been or will be realized.
whyNot.2: Maintain updates the business case with progress and forecasts.

A.q: Which step of the business case technique assesses whether the project is still worthwhile?
A.why: Check means assessing whether the project is (still) worthwhile (6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Develop explores options and builds the case in the first place.
whyNot.2: Confirm is about whether benefits have been realized.
whyNot.3: Maintain updates the case with actuals and forecasts; check judges whether it still stands.

A.q: When does confirming benefits MOSTLY take place?
A.why: Confirming benefits mostly takes place after the project has closed, although iterative releases can let some benefits be realized during it (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: In initiation the canvas is developed; benefits have not yet been delivered.
whyNot.1: Retrospectives look at ways of working, not benefit realization.
whyNot.3: Before the mandate there is no project and no business case.

B.q: Why can an agile project confirm some benefits before closure?
options: Agile projects do not need post-project reviews
Products are released iteratively during the project
The project canvas does not include a benefits section
Benefits are fixed at their full forecast level
B.why: Benefits may be realized during the project when products are delivered and released iteratively (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Post-project benefits reviews still happen; the board makes sure they are planned at closure.
whyNot.2: The canvas does contain benefits: expected, measurable, with tolerance.
whyNot.3: Benefits are fixed only at minimum viability, and that is not why they can be confirmed early.

B.q: A project manager is producing the project canvas and works through business value and expected benefits with the executive. Which step of the business case technique is this?
B.why: Considering value and benefits while producing the canvas is exploring options and gathering information for investment decisions: develop (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Confirm assesses benefits already delivered or about to be.
whyNot.1: Maintain updates an existing case with actuals and forecasts.
whyNot.2: Check judges whether the case is still worthwhile; here it is still being built.

B.q: In the 'authorize project closure' activity, what does the project board do with the project canvas?
options: Hands it to the team for a retrospective
Replaces it with the end stage report
B.why: In authorize project closure the board confirms the updated project canvas and makes sure post-project benefits reviews are covered (Table 13.4).

whyNot.1: Team retrospectives look at the last iteration's ways of working.
whyNot.2: The end stage report becomes the project dashboard; it does not replace the canvas.
whyNot.3: The board reviews and confirms the canvas at closure rather than filing it unread.

C.q:
Which two statements about the business case technique in an agile project are correct?
1. Check means assessing whether the project is still worthwhile.
2. Confirm happens once, at the final stage boundary.
3. The project canvas can be maintained as releases deliver.
4. Develop happens after closure, in benefits reviews.
C.why: Check assesses whether the project is still worthwhile (6.3.1), and the canvas is updated as the project progresses and releases deliver.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: confirm mostly happens after closure, with some confirmation during the project.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: confirm is not a single event, and develop happens before and during initiation.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: develop happens in starting up and initiation.

C.q: At the end of stage 2, the project manager updates the project canvas with actual costs, benefits already measured and new forecasts. Which step is this, and in which process does it typically happen?
options: Check, in directing a project at stage end
Develop, in starting up a project
Maintain, in managing a stage boundary
C.why: Updating the case with progress and forecasts is maintain (PRINCE2 7 5.3.1); updating the business case (project canvas) is part of managing a stage boundary.

whyNot.0: The board checks the canvas in directing a project, but updating it is the PM's maintain step.
whyNot.1: Develop builds the first canvas; this is an update of an existing one.
whyNot.3: Confirm assesses benefits realization; here the PM is updating actuals and forecasts at a stage end.

C.q: After release 3, data shows a benefit far below the minimum viability set on the canvas, and it cannot be recovered. What does the business case technique support the board in doing?
options: Waiting for post-project reviews before acting
Raising the time tolerance so more can be built
Asking the team to stop measuring benefits
Checking justification and closing early if needed
C.why: Checking whether the project is still worthwhile, using real release results, lets the board instruct premature closure if justification is lost (6.3.1, Table 13.4).

whyNot.0: Evidence is available now; continued justification is checked throughout.
whyNot.1: Time has zero tolerance by default in PRINCE2 Agile.
whyNot.2: Measurement is how benefits are confirmed; stopping it removes the evidence.

reteach.title: A garden, not a monument
reteach.question: Do you plan a garden once and walk away, or tend it as the seasons show what grows?

blocks.body: You design the garden (develop), ask each season whether it is still worth the effort (check), adjust the plan with what actually grew and what it cost (maintain), and enjoy the harvest (confirm). In agile, harvests come in small batches through the year, so you can confirm some results long before the final one.

blocks.text: Check judges; maintain updates. Confirm is about benefits, and in agile it can start during the project.

explain.body: Explore options and get the right information for investment decisions. In agile the executive leads the project canvas from the mandate in starting up, and a more detailed canvas is produced in initiation.

test.q: Who leads development of the project canvas from the mandate in starting up a project?
test.why: In 'prepare the outline business case', the executive leads development of the project canvas from the mandate (Table 13.1).

whyNot.0: The product owner manages one team's product backlog.
whyNot.2: The team coach supports one or two delivery teams.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administration and dashboards.

explain.body: Assess whether the project is (still) worthwhile: desirable, viable and achievable. The board does this when it authorizes initiation, the project and each stage.

options: Whether intended benefits have been realized
Whether the project is still worthwhile
How the team should estimate work
test.why: Check means assessing whether the project is (still) worthwhile (6.3.1).

whyNot.3: Estimation is a plans practice technique.

explain.body: Update the case with actual progress (products delivered, costs, benefits realized) and the latest forecasts. In agile, the project manager updates the project canvas at stage boundaries.

test.q: Updating the project canvas with actual costs and new forecasts is which step?
test.why: Maintain updates the business case with progress and the latest forecasts (PRINCE2 7 5.3.1).

whyNot.0: Confirm assesses whether benefits are realized.
whyNot.1: Develop builds the case at the start.
whyNot.2: Check judges whether it is still worthwhile.

explain.body: Assess whether intended benefits have been or will be realized. Mostly after closure, but iterative releases let some benefits be confirmed during the project.

test.q: Which statement about the confirm step in an agile project is correct?
options: It can start during the project as releases deliver
It replaces the check step at each stage end
It is the delivery team's job at each retrospective
It is a step completed before the project starts
test.why: Benefits may be realized during the project when products are released iteratively, although confirmation mostly follows closure (6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Check and confirm are separate steps with different questions.
whyNot.2: Retrospectives review ways of working; benefits confirmation involves the business and the board.
whyNot.3: There are no benefits to confirm before the project delivers.
